title: The Outer Banks
sources: Landsat data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey

paragraphs.text: Sometime in the night of June 2, 2026, a beach house on Ocean Drive in Buxton, North Carolina, fell into the Atlantic. It was the thirty-second house lost on this national seashore since 2020.

stat.label: Collapsed on Cape Hatteras National Seashore beaches since 2020
stat.source: National Park Service, Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Aug 2026

paragraphs.text: Twenty of them stood in Buxton and twelve in Rodanthe. Six went on a single day in September 2025. Five more went on one day that October. And four more fell in two days this February.

stat.label: Buxton houses lost on 30 September and 28 October 2025
stat.source: National Park Service, Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Aug 2026

shots.photo: File:Photo of March 13, 2023, collapsed house at 23228 East Point Dr., Rodanthe.jpg
File:Photo of debris associated with house collapse at 24131 Ocean Dr., Rodanthe - 53753242008.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Debris after a collapse, Ocean Drive, Rodanthe

paragraphs.text: This is the shore at Rodanthe in August 1985. And this is the same shore this October. We measured where the water line sits in Landsat images, year by year.
Since 1985 it has moved about a hundred and fifty-five metres inland. That is about five hundred feet, or roughly twelve feet a year.

stat.label: How far the shoreline at Rodanthe moved inland, 1985 to 2026
stat.note: About 510 feet; tides move a single day's line by tens of metres

shots.photo: File:Photo of debris associated with house collapse at 24131 Ocean Dr., Rodanthe - 53752082612.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: After a collapse, Ocean Drive, Rodanthe

paragraphs.text: It did not move evenly. By 2000 the line had already gone about a hundred metres. Then it slowed for twenty years, and since 2022 it has picked up again: about thirty metres more in four years.
These islands have always moved. What is new is what we built on them that cannot move: a lighthouse, a road, and the houses along it.

shots.photo: File:Lighthouse at Cape Hatteras National Seashore. NPS-Michael B. Edwards (18497979278).jpg

paragraphs.text: One of the three was moved out of the way. The other two are still waiting, and the rules tell them to wait. Why does the government pay for a house only after the ocean has taken it?

shots.photo: File:National Park Service employees collect house collapse debris - 52749539471.jpg
File:National Park Service employees look for house collapse debris on beach north of the Rodanthe Pier.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Searching for debris north of the Rodanthe Pier

shots.photo: File:Truck travels along beach north of Rodanthe Pier.jpg

ask.text: Would you wait for your house to fall?

paragraphs.text: The Outer Banks are barrier islands: narrow ribbons of sand between the Atlantic and the shallow sounds behind them.

The US Geological Survey describes how they move. In a storm, waves push sand over the dunes and drop it on the far side. Storm after storm, the island rolls toward the mainland. Geologists call it barrier island rollover. Wind moves sand as well, and inlets open, close and wander along the coast. Storms can also hit from behind. In 2019 Hurricane Dorian flooded North Core Banks, farther south, from the sound side, and a study led by the USGS found the island lost about eighteen percent of its sand above water.

stat.label: How a barrier island moves toward the mainland

paragraphs.text: Sometimes a storm cuts straight through. In September 2003, Hurricane Isabel opened a new inlet north of Hatteras Village, where an old inlet had closed in the 1930s.

It was about two thousand feet wide and fifteen feet deep, in three channels. The village was cut off for two months. The Army Corps of Engineers pumped sand into the gap, and the road reopened on November 22. Elsewhere Isabel buried Highway 12 under as much as three feet of sand.

stat.label: Width of the inlet Hurricane Isabel cut in September 2003

shots.photo: File:Buxton beach nourishment in progress, July 2022.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Pumping sand north of Buxton, July 2022

stat.label: Sand Isabel left on parts of Highway 12, 2003

paragraphs.text: For an island, moving is how it survives a rising sea. For a road, a lighthouse or a house on pilings, it is a disaster. And the first building here to face that choice was the tallest.

shots.photo: File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse shadow (50068811063).jpg

paragraphs.text: The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse was finished in 1870, about fifteen hundred feet from the ocean. The National Park Service calls it the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States.

shots.photo: File:Lighthouse at Cape Hatteras National Seashore. NPS-Michael B. Edwards (18497979278).jpg

stat.label: From the ocean when the lighthouse was finished, 1870
stat.source: National Park Service, Moving the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse

paragraphs.text: By 1970 the ocean was a hundred and twenty feet away. The tower before it, built in 1803 about a mile from the shore, was finally lost to a storm in 1980.

stat.label: From the ocean in 1970
stat.source: National Park Service, Moving the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse

paragraphs.text: People tried to hold the line. In 1936 the Coast Guard built groins, then gave up and moved the light to a steel tower in the woods. In the 1960s and 70s came new sand and three more groins. In 1980 the Park Service studied a seawall.

stat.label: The Coast Guard builds groins, then moves the light inland
stat.source: National Park Service, Moving the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse

stat.label: A seawall is studied to hold the old site
stat.source: National Park Service, Moving the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse

paragraphs.text: Moving it was first rejected as impractical. In 1988 the National Academy of Sciences looked at ten options and recommended moving it. It took almost another decade before Congress paid for it. In January 1997 a review by North Carolina State University endorsed the move, and money followed the next year. The tower had stood since 1870 on a floating foundation of yellow pine timbers, laid in fresh water under the sand.

shots.photo: File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse inspection 12-06-2020 - 53554408139.jpg

stat.label: Reviewed by the National Academy of Sciences, 1988: move it
stat.source: National Park Service, Moving the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse

paragraphs.text: In June 1999, crews lifted 4,830 tons of brick onto rails and pushed it five feet at a time. Sixty sensors watched the tower as it rolled. Twenty-three days later it stood 2,900 feet to the southwest. It cost 11.8 million dollars, and it was lit again on November 13. The keepers' houses had gone first, between February and April.

shots.photo: File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse Restoration Project 02-24-2024 - 53554250733.jpg

stat.label: Moved southwest in 23 days, June-July 1999
stat.source: National Park Service, Moving the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse

stat.label: Cost of the move

shots.photo: File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse shadow (50068811063).jpg

paragraphs.text: Today it stands about fifteen hundred feet from the ocean again. Here is that corner of Buxton in August 1985, and this October. Just north of the old site runs Old Lighthouse Road. One of the houses that fell this February stood on it.

shots.photo: File:FEMA - 8383 - Photograph by Mark Wolfe taken on 09-20-2003 in North Carolina.jpg

paragraphs.text: The lighthouse got out of the way. The road beside it could not, or not easily.

Highway 12 is the only road onto Hatteras Island. Its northern gate is Oregon Inlet. The Bonner Bridge crossed it from 1963. It was designed to last about thirty years and stayed in service for fifty-six. In December 2013 the current scoured the sand around its supports so badly that it was closed for ten days, and the state ran an emergency ferry instead.

shots.photo: File:Outer Banks Scenic Byway - Herbert C. Bonner Bridge and Oregon Inlet - NARA - 7720871.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Bonner Bridge over Oregon Inlet

paragraphs.text: Its replacement, the Marc Basnight Bridge, opened in February 2019: 2.8 miles long, built to last a hundred years, at a reported cost of about 252 million dollars. At its highest it rises ninety feet above the inlet.

stat.label: The Marc Basnight Bridge, opened February 2019

paragraphs.text: South of the bridge the road runs along Pea Island, a wildlife refuge, with the ocean on one side and the sound on the other. In August 2011, Hurricane Irene cut through it.

Near Rodanthe the road followed an eroding stretch called the S-curves. The fix was to leave the island. Since July 2022, a 2.4-mile bridge has carried the road out over Pamlico Sound and back. Reports put its cost at about 145 million dollars. The bridge skipped the S-curves, but not the rest of the road.

stat.label: The Rodanthe 'Jug Handle' Bridge, opened July 2022

paragraphs.text: This autumn showed what is left. On September 24 a nor'easter washed out about a thousand feet of road near the Pea Island Visitor Center. For the first time since December 2013, the state ran an emergency ferry from Rodanthe to Stumpy Point on the mainland.

The road reopened on October 3. On October 19 the ocean closed it again, this time damaging more than twelve hundred feet of pavement. The ferry came back, and by October 26 it had carried 1,451 vehicles and 2,416 passengers, around the clock. Each ferry takes only a few vehicles, and the state asked drivers for patience. The county ran park-and-ride buses at both ends. Visitors were ordered off the island.

stat.label: Pavement damaged near the Pea Island Visitor Center, October 2026
Carried by the emergency ferry by October 26

paragraphs.text: It reopened on October 29 with one lane, controlled by flaggers, behind rebuilt dunes and sandbags. The state is now discussing moving a one-mile section west. Here is that spot in August 1985, and this October. We measured about a hundred metres of retreat here since 1985. On an island this narrow, west does not go very far.

stat.label: Shoreline retreat at the Pea Island Visitor Center, 1985 to 2026

paragraphs.text: In December 2024 the Park Service sent Congress a report on its erosion hotspots. Rodanthe and Buxton are where the houses have fallen.

shots.photo: File:Photo of debris associated with house collapse at 24131 Ocean Dr., Rodanthe - 53753242008.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Debris after a collapse, Ocean Drive, Rodanthe

shots.photo: File:Photo of debris associated with house collapse at 24131 Ocean Dr., Rodanthe - 53752082612.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: After a collapse, Ocean Drive, Rodanthe

paragraphs.text: A Park Service scientist put the average loss at Rodanthe at nine to twelve feet a year between 1998 and 2022. Our own measurement since 1985 lands in the same range.

stat.label: Average yearly shoreline loss at Rodanthe, 1998-2022
stat.source: Cape Hatteras National Seashore scientist, via WRAL

paragraphs.text: In Rodanthe, Richard Foreman's house stands about twenty feet up on stilts. It was a rental. Now it stands in the middle of the beach. Four neighbouring houses have fallen in the last two years, NPR reported in September. Inside, he said, it looked as if they had just left for dinner, with everything still there. NPR counted at least half a dozen homes here in imminent danger.

shots.photo: File:National Park Service employees collect house collapse debris - 52749539471.jpg
File:National Park Service employees look for house collapse debris on beach north of the Rodanthe Pier.jpg

paragraphs.text: In Buxton, Michael McDaniel bought his house in 2011 for about half a million dollars. When he bought it, there were about two hundred and fifty feet of dune in front of it, NPR reported. If it falls, his flood insurance would pay up to 250,000 dollars for the house and up to 100,000 for what is inside. More than ninety percent of the houses that fell in Dare County since 2020 were assessed at over 250,000 dollars, NPR found.

stat.label: Dune in front of one Buxton house when it was bought in 2011

paragraphs.text: The Park Service keeps the list by address. In two days this February it was 46201, 46215 and 46219 Tower Circle Road and 46285 Old Lighthouse Road, all in Buxton. In June it was 46000 Ocean Drive.

stat.label: Buxton, collapsed overnight, 2 June 2026
stat.source: National Park Service, Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Aug 2026

paragraphs.text: When a house falls, the debris spreads along the beach. The Park Service says owners' cleanups have not always restored the beach, so it cleans up and seeks the cost back. NPR counted more than 480 tons of debris collected in eighteen months. After one Rodanthe house fell in March 2025, crews hauled about seventy truckloads off the beach in three days.

shots.photo: File:National Park Service employees collect house collapse debris - 52750036938.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Park Service crews collect debris, Rodanthe

paragraphs.text: So why are these houses left standing until they fall?
Most flood insurance for American homes comes from one place: FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program. And it pays when a house collapses, not before.

stat.label: When federal flood insurance pays for a house on a collapsing shore

shots.photo: File:National Park Service employees collect house collapse debris - 52749539471.jpg
File:National Park Service employees look for house collapse debris on beach north of the Rodanthe Pier.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Searching for debris north of the Rodanthe Pier

paragraphs.text: Foreman told NPR that if the insurer settled with him now, he would have the house torn down tomorrow. Waiting, he said, means it will fall in a storm and be scattered for miles.

shots.photo: File:Truck travels along beach north of Rodanthe Pier.jpg
File:Photo of March 13, 2023, collapsed house at 23228 East Point Dr., Rodanthe.jpg
File:Collected debris associated with March 13 house collapse.jpg

paragraphs.text: Tearing a house down costs at least thirty thousand dollars. Moving one can cost hundreds of thousands. A collapse can pay up to two hundred and fifty thousand dollars for the building and up to a hundred thousand for what is inside.

stat.label: The least it costs to tear a threatened house down

chart.title: One threatened house, in dollars
data: Owner pays to tear it down

paragraphs.text: A policy analyst at the Coastal States Organization told NPR the homeowner is incentivized to wait for collapse and get a payout. In Buxton, McDaniel put it this way: if it is teetering, you have to sit and wait for it to fall in the ocean.

It was not always like this. From 1988 to 1994, a rule called Upton-Jones paid owners to move or demolish houses that were about to fall. More than four hundred homes in twenty-seven states were moved or torn down under it. Congress repealed it in 1994. Lawmakers worried about the cost; one said that policyholder benefits come at the government's expense.

shots.photo: File:Vehicles and staff on beach collecting beach debris.jpg
File:Photo of debris associated with house collapse at 24131 Ocean Dr., Rodanthe - 53753021681.jpg
File:Volunteers clean up beach debris.jpg

stat.label: Moved or demolished under Upton-Jones, 1988-1994, in 27 states

shots.photo: File:Volunteers participate in beach debris cleanup - 52752007055.jpg

paragraphs.text: At a 1990 hearing, the man who handled those claims in North Carolina said many owners had repaired their houses instead, to rent them out another season. He saw no particular incentive for early action.

A bipartisan bill introduced in 2025 would bring a version of it back, capped at two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. As of September it was stalled in the House. FEMA says it cannot change the rule without Congress, and it did not answer NPR's question about what the waiting costs taxpayers.

stat.label: A bill to pay before collapse, stalled in the House

shots.photo: File:Collected debris associated with March 13 house collapse.jpg

paragraphs.text: Dare County's manager put the arithmetic simply. It is money they are going to spend either way, he told NPR, and it is cheaper to tear it down.

The waiting has a public cost too. NPR counted more than half a million dollars of federal and county cleanup spending since 2020. A longtime flood insurance agent told NPR that collapses leave a legacy of hazard on the beach, and that it is almost impossible to get everything.

stat.label: Federal and county cleanup spending since 2020

shots.photo: File:National Park Service employees collect house collapse debris - 52750036938.jpg

paragraphs.text: Chellie Pingree, a congresswoman from Maine, told NPR that people should not have to wait for their home to collapse into the water before they can get help.

shots.photo: File:Vehicles and staff on beach collecting beach debris.jpg
File:Photo of debris associated with house collapse at 24131 Ocean Dr., Rodanthe - 53753021681.jpg

paragraphs.text: There is another answer: bring the beach back. Between June 2017 and February 2018, Dare County pumped 2.6 million cubic yards of sand onto 2.9 miles of Buxton's shore. NPR reported that the earlier sand lasted less than three years.

shots.photo: File:Buxton beach nourishment in progress, July 2022.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Pumping sand north of Buxton, July 2022

stat.label: Sand pumped onto 2.9 miles of Buxton beach, 2017-2018

paragraphs.text: Our measurement shows it. Buxton's shoreline jumped about thirty metres out to sea. By 2024 the gain was gone, and the shore sat behind its 2014 line again.

A second round followed in 2022, with 1.2 million more cubic yards in Buxton, under a contract of about 26 million dollars for Buxton and Avon together. Now the county plans a bigger one for Buxton and Avon: up to about sixty-five million dollars if FEMA pays its share of about thirty million, or about forty-five million without it. Most of the money comes from two percent of the county's six percent tax on vacation stays, and the county wants a reserve of one and a half times a year of that tax.

stat.label: Planned Buxton and Avon beach nourishment, 2026
stat.note: About $30.4 million of it expected from FEMA

paragraphs.text: Rodanthe has no such project. A study put its cost at about forty million dollars, and the county says the village's tax base is too small to carry it.

stat.label: Estimated cost of nourishing Rodanthe's beach

paragraphs.text: A scientist at East Carolina University told NPR that beach nourishment is temporary: you are buying sand to buy time. There is no way to maintain homes where they currently are, he said. The only solution is to back off the front line.
That has started, house by house. In 2023 the Park Service bought two houses on East Beacon Road in Rodanthe, with conservation money and no taxpayer dollars, and paid 72,500 dollars to remove them.

shots.photo: File:Volunteers clean up beach debris.jpg
File:Volunteers participate in beach debris cleanup - 52752007055.jpg

stat.label: To remove two houses the Park Service bought in Rodanthe, 2023
stat.source: National Park Service, Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Aug 2026

paragraphs.text: On October 30, more than a million dollars from FEMA and the state was approved to buy three more houses in Rodanthe, if the owners agree. One is a local landmark called the Black Pearl, threatened by erosion for more than a decade. If the sales go through, the land will stay open beach.

stat.label: To buy and demolish three Rodanthe houses: FEMA $793,000, state $258,000

paragraphs.text: Not every stretch is retreating. At Avon, between the two villages, our measurement shows the shoreline about where it was in 1985.

stat.label: Shoreline change at Avon, 1985 to 2026

paragraphs.text: In 1999 the lighthouse question ended with one decision: move it. From the Academy's report to the move took eleven years. A quarter of a century later it still stands, about fifteen hundred feet from the water.

shots.photo: File:Lighthouse at Cape Hatteras National Seashore. NPS-Michael B. Edwards (18497979278).jpg
File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse inspection 12-06-2020 - 53554408139.jpg
File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse shadow (50068811063).jpg
File:Cape Hatteras Lighthouse Restoration Project 02-24-2024 - 53554250733.jpg

paragraphs.text: The road and the houses face the same question, asked again after every storm: hold the line with sand and sandbags, or move back while there is still somewhere to go.

Moving back is not free either. It means buying out owners, paying for demolition, and losing a beach town's tax base one lot at a time. Holding the line means pumping sand every few years, and the county's own finance chief says those projects will cost more as they go.

shots.photo: File:Buxton beach nourishment in progress, July 2022.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Pumping sand north of Buxton, July 2022

paragraphs.text: The Park Service expects more than a hundred homes on these islands to be at risk within a decade. At Rodanthe, our line has moved about thirty metres since 2022 alone. We will keep measuring this shore from orbit, year after year.

stat.label: At risk on North Carolina barrier islands within a decade (Park Service)

paragraphs.text: So who should decide when a house comes down: the owner, the county, or an insurer that pays only after the ocean has decided?

ask.text: Owner, county or insurer: who decides?

youtube.title: 32 Houses Fell Into the Atlantic. Insurance Paid Only After
youtube.description: Since 2020, 32 houses have collapsed into the Atlantic on Cape Hatteras National Seashore, 20 in Buxton and 12 in Rodanthe. We measured the shoreline in Landsat images from 1985 to 2026: at Rodanthe it moved about 155 metres inland. We follow the lighthouse that was moved in 1999, Highway 12 and its bridges and closures in autumn 2026, the flood-insurance rule that pays only after a house falls, and the choice between pumping sand and moving back.
youtube.pinned_comment: Owner, county or insurer: who should decide when a house on a collapsing shore comes down?
